_README: Single source of truth for all site copy. Edit text here; the components read from this file. Conventions: (1) inline links in prose use markdown [text](url); (2) `icon` fields are string keys mapped to React icons in code (github | soundcloud | spotify | instagram | linkedin); (3) `href` of value 'mailto:...' opens email; (4) section keys double as DOM ids / nav targets — don't rename without updating nav. Button/tab labels (shows/releases/collective, projects/stack/experience) are intentionally NOT here — they're UI controls, not content.

hero.elevatorPitch: a full-stack engineer building governed agentic AI and real-time collaboration tools for a payments company — and, performing as monty (us), a house and tech-house producer and dj who has headlined in brooklyn and opened and closed the #1-ranked club in the country. i've always loved making things, and these are the two i keep coming back to.

paragraphs: I grew up in New Jersey splitting time between making things and performing them — two halves that never felt separate. Before I wrote a line of code I was a competitive ice hockey player and a classically trained musician: piano, oboe, viola, drums. What held my attention was always the building, whether the result was a song, a system, or a set.

I started producing at ten on GarageBand and moved to FL Studio two years later. Early on I made rap and hip-hop beats for local artists; then dance music reorganized how I heard everything. Now I produce and DJ as Monty (US) — warm basslines, crisp percussion, a UK- and minimal-leaning take on house and tech house — and I've opened and closed for artists I grew up listening to across DC, Baltimore, and New York. In 2026 that became a residency at Transmission, a first headline night in Brooklyn, and both ends of the night at Echostage.

I studied Computer Science at the University of Maryland, where I gravitated toward audio engineering, signal processing, and machine learning — including senior research on auditory signal processing at UMD's Perceptual Interfaces & Reality Lab. Today I'm a full-stack developer in Fiserv's Global Business Solutions group, building an enterprise payments developer portal and the AI tooling behind it. A lot of what I build starts with the music. Most projects I take on solve a problem I have as an artist — a setlist optimizer, audio-analysis pipelines, the tooling that runs my own workflow.

With two close friends I co-founded [PB&J Sounds](https://pbandjsounds.com), an East Coast collective and label built around underground house, and I hold a residency with [Beatprint](https://www.instagram.com/beatprint__) at Transmission DC. My investment is in the grassroots side of this scene — small rooms, real crowds, music you have to dig for — and in owning the whole stack that supports it, from the label's website to the software that prepares my sets.

Lately my focus has been making agentic AI trustworthy: at work, a governed multi-agent delivery platform where independent AI review runs before a human sees the code and a human approves every merge; at home, models on my own hardware and small fleets of agents, with the architecture written down before the code. I work for craft, rigor, and ownership — understanding something well enough to build it myself, and building it well enough to trust it on stage or in production.

Right now, music is the priority. Production is the work that compounds — it drives the long-term growth and the bookings that follow — so most of my creative energy lives in the studio and the next room I'm trying to play. The direction I care most about pulls both halves together: machine learning and signal processing applied to sound — deep learning, on-device and edge models, the territory companies like Dolby, Bose, and Sony work in — aimed at live performance and the tools producers use to make records. I want to build the instruments and systems that change how DJs play and how records get made. The engineering and the music were never two separate careers to me. They're one practice: the code serves the sets, and the sets inform the code.

events.title: Transmission (DC)

events.title: Echostage (DC)
events.description: TWINSICK's Good Company Tour — on the bill as PB&J
events.context: Echostage is a ~3,000-capacity room in Northeast DC — repeatedly ranked the #1 club in the United States in DJ Mag's Top 100 Clubs poll, and owned by Insomniac alongside Club Glow and Soundcheck. This was TWINSICK's Good Company Tour headline date, with PB&J on the official bill alongside MOONLGHT, Sunday Scaries, and Jake Shore. The largest room on the calendar to date.

events.title: Zebbie's Garden (DC)
events.context: Martin Ikin is one of UK house's most established names — a Toolroom Records mainstay, trained jazz pianist, and Beatport's best-selling artist of 2020. Open-to-close alongside him at Zebbie's Garden covered the full arc of the night: early crowd-building through to a late peak-time close.
events.setlistNote: The "Zebs MK2" mix documents the energy from this booking and is available on pbandjsounds.com.

events.title: Flash Rooftop (DC)
events.context: Flash is one of DC's most respected underground clubs — a Funktion-One club room, a ground-floor bar, and the Green Room rooftop with its retractable top. VEGGI is an LA-based producer and DJ who fuses house, hip-hop, and indie into a genreless sound, with roots in viral production videos before the move into club and festival rooms. Direct support — the slot just beneath the headliner. A competing Club Glow show the same night drew the room lighter than a usual Flash booking, but the crowd that came stayed locked in, and the set held.

events.title: Soundcheck (DC)
events.context: Biscits (Luke Wright Jones) is a UK DJ and producer working at the center of modern tech house — he broke out with "Do It Like This" on Sonny Fodera's SOLOTOKO imprint. Soundcheck draws large crowds for international headliners; this was open-to-close on a sold-out night.

events.title: Public Art Space (NYC)
events.context: The artspace series is a recurring circuit of NYC art-space showcases — smaller capacities, longer sets, a crowd that comes for the music. The opposite end of the spectrum from the large Club Glow bookings: lower production, more room to experiment. A consistent place to test sounds that wouldn't land in a festival context.

events.title: Power Plant Live! (Baltimore)
events.context: Power Plant Live! is a large entertainment complex in Baltimore's Inner Harbor — a cluster of bars and venues that scales up its production on major nights. The Halloween mainstage was an outdoor stage to a large crowd, coordinated through the Club Glow network.

events.title: Soundcheck (DC)
events.context: Öwnboss (Eduardo Fornasa Zaniolo) is a Brazilian DJ and producer and one of Brazil's most-streamed dance acts — his "Move Your Body" with Sevek was among the most-played tracks in the world in 2022, and stays a peak-time staple worldwide. An early Soundcheck booking, and the start of a steady run of slots through the Club Glow pipeline.

events.title: Somewhere Nowhere (NYC)
events.context: Somewhere Nowhere is a boutique experience space and rooftop venue in New York City. A 4th of July show — outdoors, a long set running from afternoon into the night. One of the first significant New York bookings.

events.title: Looney's Pub (College Park)
events.context: Looney's Pub is a College Park dive bar and live music venue close to the UMD campus. Opening and closing for Jake Shore was one of the first significant local bookings — a hometown-adjacent show, and an early sign of what the DJ side could become.

projects.name: Prism
projects.description: A standalone box that splits a DJ's track into drums, bass, vocals and other while it plays, and routes each stem through the mixer's FX loop. No laptop, no cloud.
projects.longDescription:
Prism is hardware for the booth. Load a track on a CDJ and it plays as normal; Prism sees the load over Pro DJ Link and starts separating it in the background.

HTDemucs runs quantized to INT4 on a Hailo-10H AI accelerator on a Raspberry Pi 5, working through the track in 10-second chunks at about twelve times real time. A few seconds after the load the stem controls go live, and JACK2 plays the pre-extracted stems in lockstep with the CDJ's playback position. Each stem gets its own encoder on the box, or a DJM-V10 FX knob over MIDI.

The audio path is balanced XLR in and out at 24-bit/192 kHz, with a 1.9 ms round trip, because extraction never sits in the live signal path.
highlights: HTDemucs (INT4) on a Hailo-10H: stems at ~12× real time
Live 3–4 s after a track loads, detected over Pro DJ Link
JACK2 plays stems locked to the CDJ's playhead
1.9 ms round-trip audio, balanced XLR, 24-bit/192 kHz
Per-stem encoders, or DJM-V10 FX knobs over MIDI
About $565 in parts: Raspberry Pi 5 with a PREEMPT_RT kernel

projects.name: venture
projects.description: An autonomous capital-allocation agent that runs real money unattended across DeFi yield, prediction markets and paper crypto. Built around one question: how much should an agent be allowed to decide on its own?
projects.longDescription:
venture is an experiment in giving an agent real stakes and engineering the trust around them. It runs on a schedule with no one watching, so most of the design is about what it may and may not do by itself.

Money enters one way, through a single exchange account, and an allocator decides where it goes: converting to stablecoins, keeping the on-chain wallet's gas topped up, funding the prediction-market account to its target. Anything that would send money off the exchange is proposed, not executed, and waits for a human to approve it.

Strategy and safety are kept apart. Each avenue runs its own logic and reports its own health; a weekly review by Claude reads the system's history and may adjust only the crypto strategy's tunables, never the guardrails. Paper trading runs alongside the real accounts, so a change can prove itself before it touches money.

It's operated from a terminal interface — a live view of every account, history, open positions, and a setup wizard that brings each connection online in order — and every agent that touches it has its financial actions gated.
highlights: One way in for money; an allocator decides where it goes
Moves off the exchange are proposals awaiting approval
The LLM review may tune strategy, never the guardrails
Paper trading alongside real accounts, to prove changes first
Per-avenue health checks and a degraded mode
Terminal UI and a setup wizard for every connection

projects.name: superset
projects.description: Rekordbox-compatible DJ setlist optimizer. A librosa/Essentia pipeline extracts 40+ spectral, timbral, and rhythmic features per track, then KMeans/DBSCAN clustering generates flow-optimized sets with a CustomTkinter GUI.
projects.longDescription:
Superset automates the part of set preparation that doesn't require taste: curating a coherent set from a library of thousands of tracks. It applies the same audio feature extraction that powers music recommendation systems to DJ curation.

The pipeline runs locally on Apple Silicon. Rekordbox XML is parsed to extract a track catalog, then librosa and Essentia compute 40+ features per track — BPM, key, spectral centroid, timbral texture, energy envelope, and more. KMeans and DBSCAN cluster the library into vibe and energy groups, and a greedy graph traversal generates a setlist that respects harmonic mixing rules and energy arc.

The output is a rekordbox-compatible XML playlist — it drops directly into the existing DJ workflow, no intermediate steps. A CustomTkinter GUI allows interactive library exploration and manual override at any point in the process.
highlights: 40+ spectral, timbral, and rhythmic features per track via librosa + Essentia
Runs entirely on-device — no API calls, no cloud dependency
KMeans + DBSCAN dual-clustering for energy and vibe segmentation
Exports rekordbox-compatible XML playlists
CustomTkinter GUI with real-time library exploration
Genre-specific parameter modes (house, dubstep)
Optimized for Apple Silicon via MLX

projects.name: realmbot
projects.description: A test bed for Jev-style decision-making systems: a headless game client where the model only picks a tactical mode, and every call falls back to a heuristic policy on a timeout, low confidence or an outage.
projects.longDescription:
realmbot is where I test how a Jev-style decision model behaves when it's in charge of as little as possible. The model (TypeSafe AI's Jev) only chooses a tactical mode; deterministic code owns safety, movement and every required protocol reply.

Every call degrades to a heuristic policy on a timeout, low confidence or an outage, and an action gate plus a rate and cost governor sit between the model and the game. Thresholds are tuned from reliability sweeps rather than by feel, so the interesting output is the evaluation: when the model helps, when the fallback wins, and what it costs.

The game is the test harness: a private server I run, with no anti-detection work of any kind.
highlights: Tests a Jev-style model as a narrow mode picker
Heuristic fallback on timeout, low confidence or outage
Action gate and a rate/cost governor
Danger thresholds tuned from reliability sweeps
Evals: when the model helps, when the fallback wins
Private test server; no anti-detection

projects.name: brodymontag.com
projects.description: This site: a laser stage rendered as ASCII through a custom GLSL glyph pass over a three.js scene, with a CPU twin in a worker for devices without 3D, and a scroll-driven journey through both halves.
projects.longDescription:
The background is one persistent stage that survives navigation. On capable devices it's a three.js scene drawn through a custom GLSL pass that turns every 8×22 px cell into a glyph; elsewhere a CPU painter in a Web Worker draws the same figures pixel for pixel.

Scroll drives it: GSAP ScrollTrigger is the single writer, so React never re-renders on scroll. Each page has its own composition, and moving between pages morphs the figures instead of cutting them.

It holds 120 fps on a scripted scroll even with the CPU slowed six times, after a pass that moved the iridescent shimmer onto one shared clock.
highlights: Custom GLSL ASCII pass over a three.js scene
CPU twin in a Web Worker, matched pixel for pixel
GSAP as the single scroll writer: no React re-renders
Figures morph across page changes
120 fps scrolling at 6× CPU slowdown
Prerendered pages that re-render hourly

projects.name: here comes the kicker
projects.description: 3D kickball, first in the browser with three.js and no build step, now ported to Unity: pitches that roll and bounce, held-power throws, positional defense with difficulty levels.
projects.longDescription:
here comes the kicker started as a browser game: three.js, plain script files, no bundler. The work went into feel — pitches that roll and bounce, throws whose power you hold rather than fix, throws that skip in off the dirt, contact you can read, and 80s-style callouts instead of box scores.

It's now being ported to C# in Unity 6, with a deterministic simulation separated from the view, camera transitions that look ahead of the ball, a crowd and audio that react to play, and a lobby in an elevated press box above the field.
highlights: Browser original: three.js, no build step
Held-power throws; pitches roll and bounce
Positional defense with difficulty levels
Unity 6 port with a deterministic sim
Camera look-ahead, reactive crowd and audio
Avatar progression designed for multiple sessions

projects.name: agent-forge
projects.description: One canonical library of agent prompts, built into variants for Claude Code and VS Code from shared blocks, with an eval and observability layer: the fleet behind most of these projects.
projects.longDescription:
My agents used to live as drifted copies across repositories. agent-forge keeps one canonical source for each, written platform-neutral and composed from shared blocks: the orchestrator-to-worker brief format, just-in-time stack discovery, dashboard logging.

A stdlib-only build splices the blocks, emits Claude Code and VS Code variants, and fails on any unresolved placeholder. An eval layer checks agents against blueprints, and runs stream into the Subagent Dashboard, a Next.js control plane for watching parallel agents live.

Guardrails are part of the source: the agent that operates venture, for example, has every financial action gated.
highlights: One source per agent, built for two platforms
Shared blocks: briefs, discovery, logging
Build fails on unresolved placeholders
Blueprint evals and an observability rollup
Live in the Subagent Dashboard (Next.js, SSE)
Lazy skill pointers: 32% fewer tokens

projects.name: Peak_Finding_Toolbox
projects.description: Research-grade peak detector for auditory signals. Handles ABR clinical wave I–V annotation, HRTF/SOFA-format spatial audio files, and general audio onset detection with configurable thresholding.
projects.longDescription:
The Peak Finding Toolbox was developed during auditory signal processing research at the University of Maryland. Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR) measurements — short electrical signals recorded from the scalp in response to sound — require precise peak annotation across five clinical waves (I-V) to be clinically useful. Existing tools were either proprietary, inflexible, or required significant manual annotation.

The toolbox provides configurable adaptive thresholding algorithms for automated ABR wave detection, with support for the SOFA (Spatially Oriented Format for Acoustics) standard used in HRTF spatial audio research. The design philosophy: accurate enough for clinical research use, accessible enough for researchers who are not Python experts — clear interfaces, documented parameters, and sensible defaults.

The toolbox is also used for general audio onset detection, where the same thresholding and peak-picking algorithms apply beyond the neurological signal domain.
highlights: ABR wave I–V annotation with adaptive thresholding algorithms
HRTF/SOFA-format spatial audio file parsing and processing
Configurable onset detection with multiple threshold strategies
MNE and BIDS-compatible data format support
Designed for clinical and academic research environments
Accessible API — no signal processing expertise required
